summary: A landlocked country in northeastern Africa that separated from Sudan by referendum in 2011 and is one of the youngest countries in the world; the White Nile flows through it, and it is known for its pastoral culture.

ranking.name: Christianity
ranking.description: In the mid-19th century European missionaries, such as those of the Catholic Comboni Missionaries, entered the South Sudan region. During the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium of 1899–1956, Britain pursued its "Southern Policy," limiting the influence of northern Muslims and handing education over to the churches, and Christian schools produced the first generation of southern elites. In the two North–South civil wars from 1955, the Khartoum government pushed Islamization and, in 1983, Islamic law, and southerners took Christianity as an identity symbol of resistance, so the number of believers grew greatly during the wars; Catholicism and the Anglican Church are the largest denominations, and Pope Francis visited Juba in 2023.

ranking.name: Traditional beliefs
ranking.description: Nilotic peoples such as the Dinka and Nuer traditionally worship a supreme god (called Nhialic in Dinka) and communicate with the spirits through ancestors, spirit mediums and cattle sacrifice; cattle are sacred in both religion and marriage. Remote farming and pastoral areas have been less affected by missions and schools, so traditional beliefs have been preserved, and many Christians also keep traditional rituals, so the line between the two is not clear.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: Islam entered the south in the 19th century with northern Arab traders, the slave trade and the garrisons of the Turco-Egyptian regime, and later spread through the Islamization policies of the Khartoum government. Because Islam in the south was often associated with slave raiding and northern rule, few people accepted it, and Muslims are concentrated mainly in towns such as Juba, Wau and Malakal and in the northern border areas.

religion.background: The peoples of South Sudan originally followed traditional religions centered on a supreme god, ancestors and cattle sacrifice. In the 19th century northern Arab traders and slave dealers brought Islam, while at the same time European missionaries began to spread Christianity. During the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium Britain handed southern education over to the churches, and Christianity became the faith of the southern elites; in the two North–South civil wars, resistance to the Khartoum government's Islamization policy made Christianity a symbol of southern identity. After independence in 2011, the churches played an important role in mediating the civil war and providing education and health care.

ranking.name: Dinka
ranking.description: The Dinka are the most numerous ethnic group in South Sudan, distributed in the Bahr el Ghazal region and Upper Nile; Dinka belongs to the Nilotic branch of the Nilo-Saharan family, and so is the most widely spoken language. In the 19th–20th centuries missionaries created a Latin-script writing system for Dinka and translated the Bible, but dialects differ greatly from place to place, and it is still mainly spoken and used within the ethnic group.

ranking.name: Nuer
ranking.description: Nuer is the language of the Nuer, the second-largest ethnic group; like Dinka it belongs to the Nilotic branch, and it is spoken mainly in Upper Nile, Unity and Jonglei states and extends into the Gambela region of Ethiopia. The Nuer live by raising cattle, and during the civil wars large numbers of Nuer refugees fled to Ethiopia and Kenya, so the language also spread to refugee camps and overseas communities.

ranking.name: Juba Arabic
ranking.description: Juba Arabic is a pidgin that formed among soldiers of various peoples, traders and local people when the Turco-Egyptian regime set up garrisons and trading posts in the south in the 19th century, and it gradually developed into a creole. It is based on Sudanese Arabic but with greatly simplified grammar, and it has become the common language among different peoples in towns such as Juba; the number of people who can actually speak it is far greater than the number of native speakers.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: The influence of English began in the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium period, when missionary schools taught in English and produced the southern elites. At independence in 2011, the new government, to distance itself from the north's Arabic policy, made English the sole official language, used in government, courts and schools; however, very few people have English as a mother tongue, and most learn it only as a second language.

language.history: South Sudan has more than 60 indigenous languages, mostly of the Nilo-Saharan family, of which Dinka and Nuer have the most speakers. When the Turco-Egyptian regime moved south in the 19th century, Juba Arabic formed in the garrisons and trading posts and became the common language of the towns. During the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium, missionaries ran schools in English and the indigenous languages; after Sudan became independent in the 1950s–60s, the Khartoum government pushed Arabization of education, provoking strong southern resistance. At independence in 2011 English was made the official language, and the constitution also recognizes all indigenous languages as national languages.

ranking.name: Kisra (sorghum flatbread)
ranking.description: Fermented sorghum batter is spread extremely thin on a hot iron griddle to make a large flatbread with a slightly sour taste, usually torn into small pieces and dipped into stews or sauces.
ranking.history: Sorghum was domesticated thousands of years ago in the area of Sudan and Ethiopia and is the most important drought-resistant crop of the upper Nile; fermented flatbreads are common in both northern and southern Sudan. Kisra has to be made fresh every day, and traditionally women spread it sheet by sheet on the griddle early in the morning, an important part of the household division of labor. During the civil wars and famines, much of the sorghum delivered as international aid was also made into kisra, so it is regarded as the most basic daily staple of South Sudan.

ranking.name: Asida (sorghum porridge)
ranking.description: Sorghum or millet flour is cooked with water into a thick, firm dough, served in a mound and eaten with stews of okra, meat or peanut butter.
ranking.history: "Asida" is the Arabic name, and this coarse-grain dough is found from North Africa through Sudan to the Arabian Peninsula, reflecting the long exchange between the Nile Valley and the Arab world. In South Sudan it is made with locally grown sorghum and millet, and with milk or a stew it makes a filling meal, well suited to farming and herding families. Because the ingredients are cheap and keep well, asida is also one of the most common staples in refugee camps and rural areas.

ranking.name: Ful medames (stewed fava beans)
ranking.description: Dried fava beans are stewed for a long time until soft and then mashed, mixed with olive or sesame oil, cumin, salt and lemon juice, and often eaten with bread for breakfast.
ranking.history: Ful medames originated in ancient Egypt, and the "medames" in its name is believed to derive from Coptic, referring to the method of slow-cooking beans buried in hot ashes. It entered Sudan along the Nile trade routes and then reached South Sudan with northern traders and town life, becoming popular as an inexpensive breakfast in the markets and snack stalls of Juba. Although South Sudan separated politically from the north after independence, it has kept many foods in common with Sudan, and ful medames is one example.

ranking.name: Ta'amiya (fava bean fritters)
ranking.description: Soaked fava beans or chickpeas are ground with herbs and onion, formed into small balls and deep-fried, crisp outside and soft inside, often eaten in bread or with ful medames.
ranking.history: "Ta'amiya" is the Egyptian and Sudanese name for falafel; in Egypt it is traditionally made with fava beans, said to be connected with the Coptic Christian rule of abstaining from meat during Lent. This snack spread to the southern towns by way of northern Sudan and, together with ful medames, became a street breakfast combination. In South Sudan it is popular mainly in cities such as Juba that are more deeply influenced by the north, an inexpensive and filling food to eat out.

ranking.name: Mandazi (fried dough)
ranking.description: Dough kneaded from flour, sugar and coconut milk or milk is cut into pieces and deep-fried, light and slightly sweet with the aroma of cardamom, often eaten with tea for breakfast.
ranking.history: Mandazi originated on the Swahili coast of East Africa, shaped by Arab and Indian Ocean trade, and later spread along trade routes through the interior of Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. During the North–South civil wars, large numbers of South Sudanese fled to the Kakuma refugee camp in Kenya and to Uganda, and brought this snack home when they returned. When South Sudan joined the East African Community in 2016, ties with its East African neighbors grew closer, and mandazi became a common breakfast snack on the streets of Juba.
